claims.text: As-received, uncoated Q235 steel has a naturally formed, non-uniform native oxide film composed primarily of iron oxides.
The native oxide on untreated Q235 provides weak or moderate corrosion protection at room temperature.
At room temperature, the native iron oxide limits ion transport by acting as a passive barrier.
The native oxide has poor uniformity and adhesion and is therefore susceptible to disruption.
Exposure at 700–900 °C to aggressive molten salt destabilizes the pre-existing oxide scale on Q235.
Thermal-expansion mismatch and chemical interactions with molten-salt ions cause oxide dissolution and spallation.
Oxide dissolution and spallation expose fresh Q235 metal and accelerate corrosion.
Controlled annealing in air can form a more homogeneous and adherent iron oxide layer on Q235.
A homogeneous, adherent pre-annealed oxide will resist salt-induced degradation better than the native oxide.
Untreated Q235 will exhibit relatively low corrosion in a neutral aqueous environment at room temperature.
Untreated Q235 will exhibit significant mass loss and cracked, non-protective oxide scales during 700–900 °C molten-salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 samples will show reduced mass loss, less spallation, and better high-temperature corrosion resistance than untreated Q235.
The governing structural mediator is the integrity and adhesion of a Fe2O3/Fe3O4 scale.
The proposed study compares untreated and air-annealed Q235 samples under otherwise identical exposure conditions.
Mass change, SEM/EDS morphology, XRD phase composition, and oxide adhesion will be measured.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to mild or low-alloy steels lacking enough alloying elements such as chromium to form robust passive films.
The hypothesis may not apply when alloying additions or external coatings fundamentally alter the surface oxide chemistry.

Similar mass loss and oxide degradation in annealed and untreated specimens, or persistence of an intact protective native oxide at high temperature, would falsify oxide uniformity and adhesion as the governing cause.

contradictions.description: The initial state is called both “pre-exposed” and “pre-exposure/as-received.” If “pre-exposed” is meant literally rather than as a typographical error, it conflicts with the untreated baseline.
